scenes.title: Idempotency & Data-Aware Scheduling
scenes.narration: This lesson covers two pillars of reliable pipelines: writing idempotent tasks and triggering work based on data rather than the clock.

scenes.title: What idempotency means
bullets: Rerunning a task yields the same result
The foundation of safe retries and backfills
scenes.narration: A task is idempotent when running it once and running it many times produce exactly the same end state. That means no duplicate rows and no double-counting, no matter how often it executes. Idempotency is the foundation that makes automatic retries and historical backfills safe, because you can rerun any interval without fear of corrupting the data.

scenes.title: Non-idempotent versus idempotent writes

right.heading: Idempotent
points: Keyed on the run's data interval

scenes.narration: Compare two ways of writing data. A fragile task blindly inserts rows and reads the current wall-clock time, so rerunning it doubles the data and produces different results each time. An idempotent task instead scopes its write to the run's data interval, either deleting and reloading that partition or using a merge, so a rerun simply overwrites the same slice cleanly. Keying every write to the interval rather than to now is the practical trick.

scenes.title: From time-based to data-aware
bullets: Cron schedules run on the clock, blind to readiness
Data-aware scheduling triggers on data updates
scenes.narration: Traditional schedules run on the clock and are blind to whether upstream data is actually ready. Data-aware scheduling flips this: a pipeline runs when the data it depends on has been updated, not merely because a certain time arrived. In Airflow this capability is expressed through Datasets, which let one DAG signal a data update and another DAG react to it.

scenes.title: Dataset-driven scheduling
scenes.code:
from airflow.datasets import Dataset

orders = Dataset('s3://warehouse/orders')

# Producer DAG marks the dataset updated on success
load = BashOperator(task_id='load', bash_command='...', outlets=[orders])

# Consumer DAG runs whenever 'orders' is updated
with DAG(dag_id='build_marts', schedule=[orders]) as dag:
    ...
scenes.narration: This example wires two DAGs together with a Dataset. We define a Dataset representing the orders data, then a producer task lists it as an outlet, so on success Airflow marks that dataset as updated. The consumer DAG sets its schedule to that same dataset, so instead of running on a timer it runs precisely when fresh orders data lands. This replaces brittle time-guesswork with true dependency-driven triggering across DAGs.

scenes.text: Make every task idempotent and let data readiness, not the clock, trigger downstream work, and your pipelines become both retryable and always fresh.
scenes.narration: The takeaway is to make every task idempotent and to let genuine data readiness rather than the clock trigger downstream work, because together these practices produce pipelines that are safe to rerun and always operate on fresh, complete data.
